exp: An encoder converts multiple input lines (e.g. decimal or unary) into a coded binary output, which is the general mechanism used to convert one number representation into another; the other options are gate-level building blocks, not converters.
A multiplexer (MUX) selects one of several input lines and routes it to a single output line, i.e. it is a many-input-to-one-output device.
Standard ASCII is a 7-bit code (128 characters); the 8th bit in extended ASCII is a later addition/parity bit.
8421 is the natural binary weighting used in BCD (Binary Coded Decimal), so 8421 code and BCD code are the same thing.
A Karnaugh map is a graphical tool for minimizing Boolean expressions by grouping adjacent 1s, reducing the number of literals and gates needed.
By the absorption law, A + AB = A(1+B) = A*1 = A, since 1+B = 1 for any B.

The Motorola MC-6801 is a genuine 8-bit microcontroller (8-bit ALU and registers). The 8088 is a common trap: despite its 8-bit external data bus, Intel and standard texts classify it as a 16-bit processor (same 16-bit internal architecture and instruction set as the 8086). Intel 4040 is 4-bit and Pentium-I is 32-bit.
The 8085 is a single +5V supply microprocessor (unlike its predecessor 8080, which needed multiple supply voltages).
The Stack Pointer (SP) in the 8085 is a 16-bit register that holds the address of the top of the stack in memory.
Second-generation computers (roughly 1955-65) replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, giving smaller, faster, more reliable machines. ICs mark the third generation and microprocessors the fourth.
A flip-flop has two stable output states and is therefore called a bistable multivibrator.
Everyday counting uses the decimal (base-10) system, the ten digits 0-9.
Binary uses only two digits, 0 and 1, so its base (radix) is 2.
Group the binary digits into 4-bit nibbles from the right: 1101 0011 -> 1101=D, 0011=3, giving hexadecimal D3 (written D3(16) in the option, garbled to 'D316').

Effective address in indexed addressing = index register content + address field. If the address field is all 0s, EA = index register content directly, which is exactly the definition of register indirect addressing.

Base-displacement addressing both lets programs be relocated by simply changing the base register (program relocatability) and lets a short address field in the instruction reach a much larger memory space (an N-word memory with an address field shorter than log2 N bits), so both (c) and (d) hold.

Immediate addressing needs no extra memory access (the operand is embedded in the instruction), giving the minimum fetch time; indexed-indirect addressing needs an index calculation plus a further indirection through memory, giving the maximum fetch time among common addressing modes.

In indirect indexed addressing, the index value and address field are first combined (X + A) to form a pointer, and the effective operand address is the content of the memory location at that computed pointer.

150 opcodes need ceil(log2 150) = 8 bits. The 1M-byte (2^20) memory needs 20 address bits; with base-register addressing the field encoded in the instruction is (20 - 12) = 8 bits per operand, since the 12-bit base register supplies the rest. Two operand fields: 2 x 8 = 16 bits, plus the 8-bit opcode = 24 bits total.

Expanding op-code lets short opcodes serve instructions with more operands and longer opcodes serve instructions with fewer, using just enough bits for each case, so on average it produces the shortest programs.

Memory access time is defined as the time from the start of a read/write operation to its completion; memory cycle time is the extra, larger figure that includes the minimum recovery time before the next operation can start.
A good memory system needs speed, reliability, low power, durability and compactness together, so all the listed properties are desirable.
2048 = 2^11, so 11 address lines are needed to uniquely select each of the 2048 locations (the '4' in 2048x4 is the word width and doesn't add address lines).

Storing data is a memory function, accepting keyboard input is an I/O function, and arithmetic/logic is done by the ALU; the control unit itself only generates the timing/control signals that coordinate these units, so none of the listed jobs describes it.
The Program Counter (PC) always holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.

In the fetch cycle, PC's value is copied into the Memory Address Register, and the Memory Data Register is then loaded with whatever is stored at that memory location; the Instruction Register is loaded afterward from the MDR.

Condition-code bits set automatically by the CPU as a side effect of arithmetic/logic operations are kept in the flag (status) register, which the programmer can read but not fully control, i.e. it is only partially user-visible.

Booth recoding treats a run of consecutive 1s in the multiplier as (subtract at the run's first/rightmost 1, add after its last 1), which correctly expresses the run's value as a difference of two powers of two -- this is what lets negative multipliers be handled without a separate correction step.

Urgent service requests can preempt the currently running program through a hardware interrupt, through a DMA controller stealing bus cycles from the CPU, or through a bus/memory-access request in a multi-module system, so all three listed mechanisms qualify.

User (writable) microprogramming means the control store is not permanently fixed by the manufacturer; it lets the designer/user rewrite the microprogram held in control memory to define new or custom machine instructions.

In the standard fetch-execute cycle, the CPU only checks the interrupt flip-flop after it finishes executing the current instruction (not mid-fetch or on a fixed timer), and branches to the interrupt cycle if it is set.

The option text for this question has clearly been merged/corrupted during extraction -- it reads as two separate choices ('both (b) and (c) are valid' and 'none of the above statements is true') run together as a single option D, so a fifth option has been lost. The intended answer is the 'both (b) and (c) are valid' statement: a software interrupt (e.g. a trap/syscall instruction) both switches the CPU from user/problem state to supervisor state and executes a controlled jump for a known abnormal condition.

A microprogram sequencer's defining job is generating the address of the next microinstruction to fetch from control memory (including branches and subroutine returns); the other options describe supporting details of that same job.
Magnetic tape only supports sequential access -- to reach a given record you must read past everything before it.

The question is oddly worded and doesn't map cleanly onto any strong technical definition. Of the choices given, 'processing string of numbers and special symbols' is the closest to general data processing, which handles numeric and symbolic data, not just words -- but this is a weak, low-confidence pick given how vague the stem is.
Memory (RAM) is volatile/temporary working storage, while storage (disks etc.) is non-volatile/permanent.
The motherboard is the main circuit board that houses the CPU, RAM, ROM/BIOS chip, and expansion slots for add-on cards.
An OCR (Optical Character Recognition) device scans and converts printed text directly into digital text; OMR reads marked bubbles/forms, MICR reads magnetic ink characters (e.g. cheques).
A floppy disk's surface is organized into concentric circular tracks, each divided into sectors, so it has both.
CD-ROM stores data optically (using a laser to read pits/lands), which is neither semiconductor memory, a register, nor magnetic memory, so none of the given categories fits.
Instructions are actually carried out (arithmetic and logic operations) in the ALU; the control unit only directs/sequences the process and storage just holds data.
Among these, a hard disk gives direct/random access to any location, making retrieval far faster than the strictly sequential magnetic tape or the slower, lower-capacity floppy disk.
A translator (compiler/assembler/interpreter) is system software that converts programs from one language to another so the hardware can run them; it is not itself application software or hardware.
An interpreter does NOT generate an object program; it reads and executes the source statements directly (one at a time), which is exactly what distinguishes it from a compiler.
